about: Facts for stone's print-failure physics (failsim.py): convection, melt viscosity, bed adhesion and the Creality K2 profile, each with its source. A value with an assumption field is a modeling choice, not a measurement. Entries with copy_of repeat Track S's materials.json and Track T's slicer.json, citations and all, until those files are on main; failsim reads the originals first.

entries.note: Standard gravity; weight of strands, beads and parts.
entries.quote: It is a constant defined by ISO standard 80000 as 9.80665 m/s2
entries.source: Wikipedia, Standard gravity

entries.note: Convection from the part's walls in still air (fan off). The paper uses it for its PLA beads; a 0.4 mm bead loses about six times as much (failsim.churchill_chu), so stone keeps it for walls only.
entries.quote: Convective heat Transfer coefficient h 10 W·m−2K−1 Natural convection of air
entries.source: He, Zhu, Zhang, Yang, Investigation on Bridging Defects in 3D-Printed Polylactic Acid Beams Using Fused Filament Fabrication, Polymers 2026, 18(2), 261, Table 3
entries.assumption: With the fan off the part's walls lose 10 W/(m2 K), the value a paper used for beads in still air

entries.note: PLA thermal conductivity, same table; carries heat up the printed column, and checks the bead is thin enough for a lumped model (Biot number).
entries.quote: Thermal conductivity k 0.13 W·m−1K−1
entries.source: He, Zhu, Zhang, Yang, Investigation on Bridging Defects in 3D-Printed Polylactic Acid Beams Using Fused Filament Fabrication, Polymers 2026, 18(2), 261, Table 3

entries.note: PETG thermal conductivity, printed solid, at 50 to 60 C (0.211 and 0.207).
entries.source: Experimental Investigation of Thermal Conductivity of Selected 3D-Printed Materials, Materials 2025, 18(17), 3950, the 100% infill table

entries.note: PLA specific heat for the lumped bead cooling.
entries.source: Bhandari and Lopez-Anido, Discrete-Event Simulation Thermal Model for Extrusion-Based Additive Manufacturing of PLA and ABS, Materials 2020, 13(21), 4985
entries.cite: Materials 2020 13:4985 PLA and ABS thermal model

entries.note: ABS conductivity and specific heat by temperature (their Table 5, from Zhou et al.). stone averages cp from Tg up to the nozzle temperature and k from room air up to Tg. PETG has no sourced specific heat for its melt: stone uses PLA's and says so.
entries.source: Bhandari and Lopez-Anido, Discrete-Event Simulation Thermal Model for Extrusion-Based Additive Manufacturing of PLA and ABS, Materials 2020, 13(21), 4985
entries.cite: Materials 2020 13:4985 PLA and ABS thermal model

entries.note: Dry air at 1 atmosphere by temperature, taken at the mean of the strand's and the air's (the film temperature).
entries.source: Lienhard and Lienhard, A Heat Transfer Textbook, version 6.00, MIT, Table A.6

entries.note: Free convection off a horizontal cylinder, 1e-6 <= Ra <= 1e9: a strand in still air. A 0.4 mm strand loses about six times what a flat wall does, so the 10 W/(m2 K) of failsim.h_still is kept for the part's walls only.
entries.quote: Churchill and Chu recommend that eqn. (8.28) be used in the range 10^-6 <= RaD <= 10^9
entries.source: Lienhard and Lienhard, A Heat Transfer Textbook, version 6.00, MIT, eq. 8.28
entries.assumption: With the fan off every line cools as a lone strand with air all around it; the lines inside a wide ledge touch, cool slower and sag more

entries.note: Forced convection across a cylinder at Pe = Re Pr <= 0.2, where Churchill-Bernstein stops.
entries.quote: For Pe <= 0.2, the Nakai-Okazaki relation should be used
entries.source: Lienhard and Lienhard, A Heat Transfer Textbook, version 6.00, MIT, eq. 7.67

entries.note: How well a printed plastic radiates; about the same for ABS and PLA, and used for every plastic.
entries.quote: The emissivity of common 3D printing materials such as ABS and PLA were measured using a reflectivity meter and have the measured value of approximately 0.92.
entries.source: Emissivity Measurements of Additively Manufactured Materials, Los Alamos (OSTI 1341825)

entries.note: Radiation constant.
entries.source: Wikipedia, Stefan-Boltzmann law

entries.note: Forced convection across a cylinder for Re Pr > 0.2 and Re < 4000, a strand's range: the bead in the part-cooling fan's air. h = Nu k / d. Lienhard's worked example 7.8 (0.1 mm wire, Re 457) gives 10.69.
entries.quote: Below Re_D = 4000, the bracketed term [1 + (Re_D/282,000)^5/8]^4/5 is ~ 1
entries.source: Lienhard and Lienhard, A Heat Transfer Textbook, version 6.00, MIT, eq. 7.66

entries.note: Air speed over the bead with the part fan at full speed. No maker publishes it.
entries.source: stone assumption
entries.assumption: Part-cooling air speed at the nozzle, 2 to 10 m/s; 5 used. It sets the fan-on h and so how long a bead stays soft.

entries.note: PLA melt viscosity by temperature and shear rate: eta0 = D1 exp(-A1 (T - T*) / (A2 + T - T*)), eta = eta0 / (1 + (eta0 rate / tau*)^(1 - n)). Fitted to NatureWorks Ingeo 3251D, an injection grade; filament PLA is close but not the same.
entries.quote: Table 2 Data-fitted Cross-WLF parameters of the PLA 3251D. A1 16.71 A2 (K) 51.60 D1 (Pa*s) 2.045 × 10^7 D3 (K/Pa) 0 T* (K) 373.15 n 0.3846 τ* (Pa) 1.29 × 10^5
entries.source: Pricci, Physics-Based Predictive Modeling of Gravity-Induced Sagging in Support-Free Pellet Additive Manufacturing, Polymers 2025, 17(21), 2858, Table 2

entries.note: ABS melt viscosity, capillary rheometer, Hatchbox black ABS filament. Another group fits 43,900 Pa s for a different ABS at 240 C from stretching tests (arXiv 2311.05158 Table 2), 22 times this: rubber-filled melts stiffen at slow rates, and stone does not model that.
entries.source: Colon, Kazmer, Peterson, Seppala, Characterization of Die-Swell in Thermoplastic Material Extrusion, Additive Manufacturing 2023 (NIST), Table 1
entries.assumption: ABS melts as a capillary rheometer measured it (Hatchbox black ABS); stretching tests on another ABS read 22 times stiffer at slow rates, which would sag less

entries.note: PETG melt viscosity at its print temperature, weight-averaged over the modes of a Giesekus fit to shear and stretch tests.
entries.quote: PET-G ... 240 (Table 1); Avg. eta 600 (Table 2)
entries.source: Assessing nozzle flow dynamics in Fused Filament Fabrication through the parametric map alpha-lambda, arXiv 2311.05158, Tables 1 and 2
entries.assumption: PETG's viscosity is one fit (600 Pa s at 240 C, the weighted mean of its 3 modes: the sum a slow sag feels is 600 to 1800, so it may sag less and drag on the nozzle up to 1.8 times as hard) moved to other temperatures by the universal WLF constants, thinning with speed as PLA does

entries.note: Universal WLF constants, measured from the glass transition: used only to move PETG's one viscosity.
entries.quote: universal constants C1 = 17.44 and C2 = 51.6 K when the reference temperature is Tg
entries.source: Wikipedia, Williams-Landel-Ferry equation

entries.note: A viscous beam bends like an elastic one with E replaced by 3 eta and deflection by its rate: stone's soft-bead droop.
entries.quote: For a Newtonian Fluid, the Trouton ratio equals three.
entries.source: Wikipedia, Extensional viscosity

entries.note: Tensile pull-off strength of PLA printed on aluminum, over their 16 treatments and bed temperatures; stone uses the lowest for the tip check (force over the whole footprint). No paper measured PEI or glass this way; treated aluminum stands in.
entries.quote: The highest tensile adhesion strength was obtained with acid etching at 65 °C (1.71 MPa) ... The lowest value was recorded for acid etching at 85 °C (0.40 MPa)
entries.source: Campos-Jurado, Rodriguez-Alabanda, Guerrero-Vacas, Manufacturing of Polymer-Metal Composite by Fused Filament Fabrication: Adhesion of PLA and PETG on Aluminum, Polymers 2025, 17(16), 2210
entries.cite: Polymers 2025 17:2210 PLA and PETG on aluminum

entries.note: Lap-shear strength of the same PLA on aluminum; the lowest is used for the slide check.
entries.quote: For PLA, the highest shear adhesion strength was obtained with acid etching at 65 °C (3.92 MPa) ... dropping to a minimum of 0.52 MPa (fine sanding, 85 °C)
entries.source: Campos-Jurado, Rodriguez-Alabanda, Guerrero-Vacas, Manufacturing of Polymer-Metal Composite by Fused Filament Fabrication: Adhesion of PLA and PETG on Aluminum, Polymers 2025, 17(16), 2210
entries.cite: Polymers 2025 17:2210 PLA and PETG on aluminum

entries.note: Peak 90 degree peel force of a printed PLA strip on borosilicate glass (DIN EN 28510-1 style test). On Pertinax PLA peaked at 160 N. stone turns the peak into an edge stress with Hetenyi's beam on an elastic foundation (failsim.hetenyi).
entries.quote: The maximum was measured for PLA with a value of 231 N.
entries.source: Laumann, Spiehl, Doersam, Device for measuring part adhesion in FFF process, HardwareX 2022, 11, e00258 (CC BY)

entries.note: Polypropylene, a low surface energy plastic, on the same glass (about 4 N) and Pertinax (7.8 N maximum). Its ratio to PLA is stone's dirty-plate factor.
entries.quote: The adhesion forces for the material pairing PP - borosilicate glass are about 4 N ... The maximum adhesion force was measured for PLA with a value of 160 N while polypropylene (PP) only adheres with a maximum of 7.8 N.
entries.source: Laumann, Spiehl, Doersam, Device for measuring part adhesion in FFF process, HardwareX 2022, 11, e00258 (CC BY)

entries.note: PETG (Filamentworld) on borosilicate glass, average of the peak forces.
entries.quote: PETG has an adhesion force between 94 N and 107 N with an average of 102 N.
entries.source: Laumann, Spiehl, Doersam, Device for measuring part adhesion in FFF process, HardwareX 2022, 11, e00258 (CC BY)

entries.note: ABS on borosilicate glass, read off Fig. 76 by eye: the bar, of the peak forces, is at 60 N, its error bar 54 to 66.
entries.quote: In Fig. 76 the observed maximum forces for each build surface and filament are plotted.
entries.source: Laumann, Spiehl, Doersam, Device for measuring part adhesion in FFF process, HardwareX 2022, 11, e00258 (CC BY)

entries.note: Glass plate temperature of the peel tests, Table 5.
entries.quote: PLA 230 220 230 60 70 50 ... PETG 250 230 230 100 96 96 ... ABS 270 230 230 130 125 125 (nozzle then build platform temperature, on brass, Pertinax and glass)
entries.source: Laumann, Spiehl, Doersam, Device for measuring part adhesion in FFF process, HardwareX 2022, 11, e00258 (CC BY)

entries.note: Width and thickness of the peeled strip. The paper prints at 0.5 mm layers with a 1 mm nozzle; the strip size is only in its Fig. 52.
entries.quote: nozzle diameter 1.0 mm, filament diameter 1.75 mm, layer height and first layer height 0.5 mm
entries.source: Laumann, Spiehl, Doersam, Device for measuring part adhesion in FFF process, HardwareX 2022, 11, e00258 (CC BY)
entries.assumption: Strip 25 mm wide (the width of an ISO 8510-1 / DIN EN 28510-1 peel specimen) and one 0.5 mm layer thick.

entries.note: Dirty-plate factor: a plate with skin oil or dust holds the part the way a poorly wetting plastic holds a clean plate. Computed from the peel data: PP / PLA = 4 / 231 = 0.017 on glass, 7.8 / 160 = 0.049 on Pertinax. stone uses the milder 0.049, so a dirty plate that fails at 0.049 fails at 0.017 too.
entries.source: Laumann, Spiehl, Doersam, Device for measuring part adhesion in FFF process, HardwareX 2022, 11, e00258 (CC BY)
entries.assumption: A contaminated plate keeps the same fraction of its hold as PP keeps of PLA's on a clean plate.

entries.value: end of a long beam on an elastic foundation: y = 2 P lambda / k under an end force P, y = 2 M0 lambda^2 / k under an end moment M0, lambda = (k / 4EI)^(1/4)
entries.note: The first layer is the foundation (k = E b / t1 per unit length, E of the part itself); the stack above it is the beam. Edge peel stress = k y / b. For a peel strip of width b and thickness h pulled at its end: sigma = 2 P lambda / b. For the part's stack see failsim.warp_rule. The OCR of the scan is cleaned up in the quote.
entries.quote: Concentrated Force at One End ... Deflections at the end points: y = (2Pλ/k) (Sinh λl Cosh λl − sin λl cos λl) / (Sinh² λl − sin² λl) ... Concentrated Moment at One End ... y = (2M0λ²/k) (Sinh² λl + sin² λl) / (Sinh² λl − sin² λl) ... λ = ⁴√(k/4EI)
entries.source: M. Hetenyi, Beams on Elastic Foundation (1946), archive.org scan, eqs. 39 and 40 (finite beam, free ends; both reduce to the long-beam values when lambda l is large)

entries.value: sigma_edge = min(2 M lambda^2, 6 M / d^2), M = sum of sigma(T) z t over the layers within d of the plate
entries.note: Corner lift, worked on the perimeter walls, which the profile prints solid through the whole height (failsim.section_rule). A layer is stress-free while above Tg; below it, at its present temperature T (failsim.column_rule), it carries sigma(T) = alpha x integral of E dT from T up to Tg, read on the measured stiffness curve. At the free edge the plate must hold the layers' pull and its moment about the plate, M per mm of edge. Hetenyi's end moment on the stack, with the first layer at the plate temperature as the foundation, gives 2 M lambda^2 (failsim.hetenyi). That beam must be thin against its bending length 1/lambda; once the stack is deeper, the moment spreads over an edge zone at least one stack depth d long (failsim.saint_venant), and the flexure formula puts the zone's peak at 6 M / d^2 (failsim.flexure). For one stress through the stack that is sigma x min(sqrt(3 n), 3): the old sqrt(3 n) rule for the first layers, held at 3 sigma once the stack is deeper than 3 layers. Only layers within d = min(height, the footprint's narrowest width) of the plate load it. The corner lifts when the edge stress passes the bond (failsim.bond_hot) times the plate factor.
entries.source: stone model from failsim.hetenyi, failsim.saint_venant, failsim.flexure and materials data
entries.assumption: Linear elastic with no stress relaxation, the steady temperature after each layer, and the walls curling on their own footprint without help from the infill inside them: each makes stone call a lift sooner than a real print. The edge zone of a deep stack is taken as one stack depth long.

entries.note: Flat face of a 0.4 mm nozzle that drags over the top layer; the drag is the melt's shear stress on it.
entries.source: stone assumption
entries.assumption: A 0.4 mm nozzle's flat tip is about 1.0 mm across.

entries.note: Drag coefficient of a long cylinder across an air stream, read off the curve through his points by stone (about 3%): wires of 0.05, 0.1 and 0.3 mm, a strand's size, below Re 600. Below Re 0.5 it follows Lamb's formula, Cd = 8 pi / (Re (2.002 - ln Re)), as his figure does.
entries.quote: The drag of small cylinders (up to 8 mm. in diameter) was determined by suspending each one vertically in the air stream as a long wire
entries.source: C. Wieselsberger, New Data on the Laws of Fluid Resistance, NACA Technical Note 84, 1922, Fig. 1

entries.note: Air blowing along a thin thread, as in fiber spinning: Kase and Matsuo measured it on a heated 0.2 mm wire, 0.5 < Re < 50. A strand straight under the part fan is at Re 100, a little past that. h_strand takes the larger of this and the air across it.
entries.quote: Nu=0.42.Re0.344 Kase and Matsuo [1965] Found by simulation of electrically heated 0.2 mm heated wire for 0.5<Re<50
entries.source: M. Golzar, Melt Spinning of the Fine PEEK Filaments, TU Dresden, 2004, Table 5.2.2 (p. 83), from S. Kase and T. Matsuo, J. Polym. Sci. A 3, 1965

entries.note: How much wider than the bore a strand comes out. ABS at a 0.4 mm nozzle: 1.17 (0.9 mm3/s) to 1.45 (10 mm3/s) at 200 C, 1.12 to 1.185 at 250 C.
entries.quote: The minimum swell ratio is 1.12, for a volumetric flow rate of 0.9 mm3/s and a hot end temperature setpoint of 250 C, and the maximum swell ratio is 1.45, for a volumetric flow rate of 10 mm3/s and a hot-end temperature setpoint of 200 C
entries.source: Colon, Kazmer, Peterson, Seppala, Characterization of Die-Swell in Thermoplastic Material Extrusion, Additive Manufacturing 2023 (NIST), section 3
entries.assumption: A strand comes out 1.2 times as wide as the bore, whatever the plastic, flow and heat (measured on ABS: 1.12 to 1.45)

entries.note: Two like bodies brought together meet at the mean of their temperatures. A strand welds to the plastic it lands on when that mean is above the glass transition.
entries.source: stone model; the mean is Carslaw and Jaeger, Conduction of Heat in Solids, section 2.16
entries.assumption: A strand stays where it lands on plastic if their mean temperature is above the glass transition; the plastic below is taken at the air's, so one just printed holds better than this says

entries.note: How far to the side of the nozzle the part fan's air blows down at failsim.fan_air_speed; past it, and above the nozzle, the air is still. A jet keeps its speed for about six of its own widths, so it is not slowed on its way down here. No maker publishes any of it.
entries.source: stone assumption
entries.assumption: The part fan blows straight down at full speed from the nozzle to what is below it, within 10 mm to the side, and not at all past that

entries.note: Friction of a soft strand on the bed or the part, in the falling-strand model.
entries.source: stone assumption
entries.assumption: Coulomb friction 0.5 on the bed and on the part: how far a fallen strand slides, and what the nozzle drags or draws thin against.

entries.note: Share of the plastic extruded with nothing under the nozzle that stays on the nozzle and heater block (blob_on_nozzle); the rest falls as strands.
entries.source: stone assumption
entries.assumption: Half of what is extruded into air stays on the nozzle.

entries.value: a = catenary constant with sag(L_usable) = one layer height
entries.note: A bridge strand hangs as a catenary z = a (cosh(x/a) - 1) with one constant a for the material: the one that sags exactly one layer at the slicer's usable bridge length (failsim.max_bridge_length). Longer spans sag more than a layer: the next layer has nothing to land on.
entries.source: stone model from failsim.max_bridge_length
entries.assumption: At the usable bridge length a bridge sags one layer height; the catenary constant is the same for every span.

entries.note: A ledge whose tip droops one layer height or more leaves the next layer nothing to print on (kind supports). Half a layer or more shows (kind droop): a line's rounded side already hides about half its height (OrcaSlicer's line is a rectangle with round ends).
entries.source: stone model
entries.assumption: Droop of one layer fails the ledge; half a layer is the smallest droop that shows.

entries.value: predict positions under gravity, project segment lengths, collide with the ground, apply friction, set velocity from the position change
entries.note: The falling strand: a chain of short segments solved by position based dynamics.
entries.source: Mueller, Heidelberger, Hennix, Ratcliff, Position Based Dynamics, Journal of Visual Communication and Image Representation 18(2) 2007, 109-118
entries.cite: Mueller et al. 2007 Position Based Dynamics

entries.note: Measured from the bed: a face sloping less than 30 deg from horizontal (more than 60 deg from vertical) gets support. The Creality K2 0.20mm Standard profile keeps 30. stone turns it into a reach per layer: layer height x tan(60 deg), 0.35 mm at 0.2 mm layers.
entries.quote: Support will be generated for overhangs whose slope angle is below the threshold. The smaller this value is, the steeper the overhang that can be printed without support.
entries.source: OrcaSlicer src/libslic3r/PrintConfig.cpp, support_threshold_angle (default 30)

entries.note: A print profile setting, not a filament one: OrcaSlicer's K2 profiles use 10 mm for PLA and PETG alike. PETG bridges sag more than PLA in practice; stone keeps 10 mm for both and says so (assumption that the slicer's limit holds for PETG).
entries.quote: This is the maximum length of bridges that don't need support. Set it to 0 if you want all bridges to be supported, and set it to a very large value if you don't want any bridges to be supported.
entries.source: OrcaSlicer src/libslic3r/PrintConfig.cpp, max_bridge_length (default 10); resources/profiles/Creality/process/0.20mm Standard @Creality K2 0.4 nozzle.json (10)

entries.value: stable while the center of mass is over the support polygon
entries.note: A part standing on the bed stays up on its own only while its center of mass, seen from above, is inside the convex hull of its first layer. stone checks it for the part as printed so far, at every layer.
entries.quote: its support polygon is a horizontal region over which the center of mass must lie to achieve static stability. For example, for an object resting on a horizontal surface (e.g. a table), the support polygon is the convex hull of its "footprint" on the table.
entries.source: Wikipedia, Support polygon

entries.value: a self-balanced load fades within about one section width of where it acts
entries.note: Why the plate does not feel every layer of a tall part: a layer's shrink pull is balanced by the layers just under it, so its effect fades with distance from the layer.
entries.quote: the difference between the effects of two different but statically equivalent loads becomes very small at sufficiently large distances from load.
entries.source: Wikipedia, Saint-Venant's principle
entries.assumption: A sufficiently large distance is the footprint's narrowest width: layers higher than that above the plate do not load it. An edge moment on a stack deeper than Hetenyi's bending length spreads over at least one stack depth.

entries.value: sigma_max = M c / I = 6 M / d^2 for a strip d long under a moment M per unit width
entries.note: The edge zone of a deep stack (d long, per mm of edge) pressed and lifted by the moment M: the peak is M / S with S = I / c, and for a d long rectangle c = d / 2, I = d^3 / 12, so S = d^2 / 6.
entries.quote: For the case where a beam is doubly symmetric, c1=c2 and we have one section modulus S=I/c.
entries.source: Wikipedia, Euler-Bernoulli beam theory

entries.value: steady conduction up the printed column: k x printed area / t between layers, h x exposed area to the air, the first layer's base at the plate temperature
entries.note: The part is a fin standing on the plate. Each layer passes heat to the next through the share of it the profile prints (failsim.section_rule) and loses heat to the air through its exposed side and top faces. The temperatures after each layer are the steady solution of that chain.
entries.quote: the tip can be exposed to convective heat transfer, insulated, held at a constant temperature, or so far away from the base as to reach the ambient temperature.
entries.source: Wikipedia, Fin (extended surface)
entries.assumption: Steady temperatures after each layer, with no reheat from the new bead; the plate holds the first layer at its set temperature; air at the chamber temperature, or failsim.room_air on an open printer.

entries.note: Heat loss from the faces of a printing part to the air, with the part fan on (failsim.h_still with it off). The same paper's FE model of PLA and ABS parts uses it on every exposed face.
entries.quote: A convective heat transfer coefficient of 100 W·m−2·K−1 was assumed for this study.
entries.source: Bhandari and Lopez-Anido, Discrete-Event Simulation Thermal Model for Extrusion-Based Additive Manufacturing of PLA and ABS, Materials 2020, 13(21), 4985
entries.cite: Materials 2020 13:4985 PLA and ABS thermal model
entries.assumption: The part fan gives every exposed face of the part this h. Between 40 and 459 W/(m2 K) (the bead's fan h at full speed, failsim.churchill_bernstein) on every face, each of stone's warp test cases keeps its verdict but one: ABS 150 x 150 x 10 mm on an open printer comes loose from 100 up and holds at 40 (margin 1.11). PLA there keeps a margin of 1.53 to 1.83.

entries.note: Air around a part on an open printer (no enclosure).
entries.quote: A temperature of 25 °C was used as the environmental temperature.
entries.source: Bhandari and Lopez-Anido, Discrete-Event Simulation Thermal Model for Extrusion-Based Additive Manufacturing of PLA and ABS, Materials 2020, 13(21), 4985
entries.cite: Materials 2020 13:4985 PLA and ABS thermal model
entries.assumption: An open printer's air is at room temperature, 25 C, with no draft beyond the part fan.

entries.value: solid within the wall loops' width of a layer's edge and within the top and bottom shell layers; sparse infill counts at its density
entries.note: The printed section: walls two loops wide (0.42 + 0.45 mm), 3 bottom and 5 top solid layers over any uncovered face, and 15% grid infill elsewhere (failsim.k2_shells, failsim.k2_widths). It sets how much of each layer conducts heat up the column. The corner sits on the walls, which are solid through the whole height, so the lift is worked on a solid section.
entries.source: stone model from failsim.k2_shells and failsim.k2_widths
entries.assumption: Sparse infill conducts in proportion to its density. The first layers of a part count as bottom shell.

entries.note: Peak force to knock a PLA cylinder off a polyimide film at each plate temperature (Tr), the mean of the parts printed at 60 and at 70 C, read off Fig. 3 (a) and (b); their PLA softens at about 60 C. On bare glass the same parts let go below 40 C.
entries.quote: bed adhesion is maximized between 60 and 70 °C ... transition temperature of PLA is ∼60 °C ... for PI, heating after printing may be more effective than cooling at lowering Fr. In particular, Fr only decreased ∼50% when testing on PI-coated glass when Tr < Tp. However, for Tr > Tp, decreases in Fr of 80 to 90% were observed.
entries.source: Snapp, Gongora, Brown, Increasing Throughput in Fused Deposition Modeling by Modulating Bed Temperature, Journal of Manufacturing Science and Engineering 2021, 143(9), 094502, Fig. 3

entries.value: bond = min(peel stress, tensile_z) x min(1, hold(max(T_plate, T_peel) - Tg) / hold(T_peel - Tg)) x plate factor
entries.note: hold is failsim.hold_curve. PLA was peeled at 50 C (11 C under its Tg): an 80 C plate holds 0.82 of that, and a 60 C plate counts as no better, though the curve says 1.5 times. The curve is of parts that cooled after printing, so it says nothing of a colder plate. PETG and ABS were peeled 30 and 24 C past their Tg, the weakest part of the curve, so their measured force stands at every colder plate. A plate is never credited with more than was measured.
entries.source: stone rule from failsim.peel.* and failsim.hold_curve
entries.assumption: The plate holds what the peel test on glass measured, less on a plate so warm that PLA on polyimide held less (PETG and ABS by the same curve, past their own Tg), never more than the plastic's strength between layers as tested at room temperature. PETG and ABS were peeled on plates 30 and 24 C past their Tg, where they hold least, so on a colder plate 'comes loose' can be a false alarm. How much less a first layer laid on a cold plate sticks is not modeled

entries.note: Walls, solid layers and infill of the K2 0.20mm Standard profile. OrcaSlicer's own defaults are 2 walls, 3 bottom, 4 top and 20% infill; the K2 profile raises the top to 5 and lowers infill to 15%.
